Priscilla and Aquila
pris-SIL-la and a-KWIL-a
proper noun phrase
Priscilla: Greek Priskilla, diminutive of Priska (Roman; Latin meaning ancient, venerable); Aquila: Latin Aquila, “eagle.” The Jewish-Christian married couple who became Paul’s tentmaking colleagues and church-planting partners in Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome; one of the most fully-documented couple-ministries in the NT.

See also: Priscilla and Aquila

Biblical Definition

Priscilla and Aquila are the Jewish-Christian married couple who became Paul’s tentmaking colleagues, church-planting partners, and Apollos’s teachers—one of the most fully-documented and pastorally exemplary couple-ministries in the NT. They are named together in six NT passages (Acts 18:2, 18, 26; Rom 16:3-4; 1 Cor 16:19; 2 Tim 4:19), always together, with Priscilla named first four of the six times (notable for the social conventions of the era, suggesting either her social prominence or her ministerial leadership or both). Their narrative spans several major NT moments. First, the meeting with Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:1-3). Aquila was a Jew born in Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome (apparently around AD 49, in connection with the Roman historical record of Jewish-Christian disputes in the Roman synagogues). Paul met them in Corinth, found that they were of the same trade (tentmakers), and abode with them, working at the trade through the week and preaching in the synagogue on the Sabbaths. The relationship that began as professional-coworker and lodging-host became a substantial ministerial partnership across the remainder of Paul’s ministry. Second, the journey to Ephesus (Acts 18:18). When Paul departed Corinth for Syria, Priscilla and Aquila accompanied him. They were left at Ephesus while Paul went on; their ministry in Ephesus became one of the substantial NT episodes. Third, the instruction of Apollos (Acts 18:24-26). The eloquent Alexandrian-Jewish Christian Apollos came to Ephesus, mighty in the scriptures, fervent in spirit, teaching diligently the things of the Lord—knowing only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila heard him, took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly. The detail is significant: they did not publicly correct him (which would have humiliated a learned man and damaged his ministry); they took him aside privately and instructed him more fully. Apollos subsequently became one of the great early-church teachers (1 Cor 1:12; 3:4-6; 4:6; 16:12; Titus 3:13). The pastoral substance of Priscilla and Aquila’s private-instruction-of-Apollos approach is a model for the recovery-and-improvement of capable-but-incomplete teachers. Fourth, the host-of-the-church-in-their-house pattern. Romans 16:3-5 mentions the church that is in their house in Rome (they had apparently returned after Claudius’s edict expired); 1 Corinthians 16:19 mentions the church that is in their house in Ephesus. They twice hosted a meeting-church in their home, demonstrating one of the chief NT patterns of church-life. Fifth, Paul’s grateful acknowledgment of their substantial sacrifice for him. Romans 16:3-4: greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus: Who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not I only give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles. At some point (the specific incident is not recorded) they had risked their lives for Paul; the Pauline-and-universal church gratitude is the warm appreciation of their substantial sacrifice. The Priscilla-and-Aquila portrait is therefore one of the great NT pictures of a married Christian couple’s coordinated, mutually-engaged, substantial ministerial partnership—tentmaking colleagues, fellow-travelers, fellow-teachers, fellow-hosts, willing-to-suffer fellow-helpers in the gospel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Priscilla and Aquila were the Jewish-Christian married couple who became Paul’s tentmaking colleagues and church-planting partners; they hosted the church in their house in both Ephesus and Rome, instructed Apollos more perfectly in the way of God (Acts 18:26), and risked their lives for Paul (Rom 16:3-4); one of the most fully-documented and pastorally exemplary couple-ministries in the NT.

expand to see more

PRISCILLA — Roman name (diminutive of Priska, “venerable”) of the wife of Aquila; mentioned 6 times in the NT, 4 of those times named before her husband.

AQUILA — Latin name (“eagle”) of the Jewish-Christian tentmaker of Pontus, husband of Priscilla, Paul’s colleague and church-planting partner across Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome.

Key Scripture

Acts 18:2-3 — "And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them. And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers."

Acts 18:26 — "And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly."

Romans 16:3-5 — "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus: Who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not I only give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles. Likewise greet the church that is in their house."

1 Corinthians 16:19 — "The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house."

Modern Corruption

The Priscilla-and-Aquila doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the contemporary gender-politics readings that have used Priscilla’s frequent listing-first as proof-text for various positions on women’s teaching ministry—both the egalitarian over-extension that has used her example to argue for women’s ordination to authoritative teaching offices, and the complementarian over-correction that has minimized her substantive teaching role in the Apollos-instruction.

expand to see more

The contemporary gender-politics readings have, in various ways, used the Priscilla-and-Aquila narrative as proof-text for positions on women’s teaching ministry the apostle did not directly address in their portrait. The egalitarian over-extension cites Priscilla’s frequent listing-first and her role in instructing Apollos as evidence that women may hold authoritative teaching offices in the church on equal footing with men. The complementarian over-correction has often minimized Priscilla’s substantive teaching role in the Apollos-instruction, treating her as merely her husband’s passive co-listener. The biblical narrative is more careful than either reading. Priscilla’s frequent listing-first is striking but does not necessarily establish her in an authoritative office over Aquila; her substantive participation in the private instruction of Apollos is clear but is described as a husband-and-wife joint ministry (they took him unto them, and expounded), not as a solo authoritative-teaching event. The recovery is the careful reading: Priscilla and Aquila are presented as a substantial couple-ministry, with both partners actively engaged in teaching-and-discipling work, in the context of the broader apostolic ecclesiology that distinguishes the various ministries and offices the NT establishes.

The deeper loss in much contemporary preaching is the substantive couple-ministry pattern the Priscilla-and-Aquila portrait presents. The married Christian couple as a coordinated ministerial team is one of the great NT patterns, with this couple as its most fully-documented example. Tentmaking colleagues (sharing a trade and a household economy); fellow-travelers (relocating together as the gospel required); fellow-teachers (jointly instructing Apollos); fellow-hosts (twice hosting the church in their house); willing-to-suffer fellow-helpers (risking their lives for Paul). The contemporary church often presents marriage in either traditional roles-divided terms (the husband’s ministry, the wife’s separate ministry) or in egalitarian autonomous-careers terms (each spouse pursuing his or her own vocation); the Priscilla-and-Aquila pattern presents a third option that the NT favorably documents: the coordinated couple-ministry in which the married couple together engage substantive ministerial work as a single coordinated unit. The recovery is the recovery of the couple-ministry pattern as one of the substantial NT models for Christian marriage and ministry.

Hebrew Roots

Greek Priskilla (from Latin Priska, venerable) and Latin Aquila (eagle); the Jewish-Christian married couple from Pontus and Italy who became Paul’s tentmaking colleagues and substantial ministerial partners across Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome; instructed Apollos privately (Acts 18:26), hosted churches in their house in two cities, and risked their lives for Paul (Rom 16:3-4); one of the most fully-documented and pastorally exemplary couple-ministries in the NT.

expand to see more

Greek Priskilla (G4252) — Priscilla (mentioned 6 NT times; Acts 18:2, 18, 26; Rom 16:3; 1 Cor 16:19; 2 Tim 4:19).

Greek Akulas (G207) — Aquila (the same 6 NT references, paired with Priscilla).

Greek skēnopoios (G4635) — tentmaker (Acts 18:3, the shared trade of Paul, Priscilla, and Aquila).

Greek akribōs (G199) — more accurately, more perfectly (Acts 18:26, of their instruction of Apollos more perfectly).
